analysis.morphology: Qal wayyiqtol, third person masculine singular, with prefixed וַ־

draft.change: Link the existing Abram article to אבה through its father element and add Genesis 12:4 as an example.
draft.definition: Abram, son of Terah, later named Abraham. The name means “exalted father.”
draft.evidence: Genesis 12:4 repeats the name אַבְרָם when giving Abram’s age at departure. The name’s אָב element belongs to Haqor’s אבה article.

analysis.evidence: וַיֹּאמֶר לְאַבְרָם means “he said to Abram.” The masculine singular address תֵּדַע (“you will know”) and זַרְעֲךָ (“your offspring”) confirm that Abram is the addressee.
analysis.morphology: The prefixed preposition לְ marks the addressee. אַבְרָם is a masculine personal name.
analysis.sense: Abram, the son of Terah later named Abraham

analysis.evidence: The phrase יָדֹעַ תֵּדַע means “know for certain.” The כִּי clause gives the content of what Abram is to know: his descendants will live as foreigners in a land that is not theirs.
analysis.morphology: Qal infinitive absolute. It precedes תֵּדַע, the finite verb of the same root, to emphasize certainty.
analysis.sense: to know that something is the case

analysis.evidence: The preceding infinitive absolute יָדֹעַ emphasizes תֵּדַע. The following כִּי clause states what Abram is to know for certain, that his descendants will live as strangers in a land that is not theirs.
analysis.morphology: Qal imperfect, second person masculine singular, addressed to Abram. The initial ת marks the person of the verb.
analysis.sense: to know that something is the case

analysis.evidence: After יָדֹעַ תֵּדַע (‘you shall surely know’), כִּי introduces what Abram is to know, beginning with גֵר יִהְיֶה זַרְעֲךָ (‘your offspring will be strangers’).
analysis.morphology: Uninflected Hebrew conjunction with no prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: that (what is seen, known or said)

analysis.evidence: The phrase בְּאֶרֶץ לֹא לָהֶם, “in a land that is not theirs,” explains the status of Abram’s offspring. They will live there as outsiders.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular absolute common noun serving as the predicate of יִהְיֶה. Its subject is the collective singular זַרְעֲךָ, “your offspring.”

analysis.evidence: In גֵר יִהְיֶה זַרְעֲךָ, the predicate גֵר describes the future status of Abram’s offspring. The phrase בְּאֶרֶץ לֹא לָהֶם explains that they will be strangers in a land that is not theirs.
analysis.morphology: Qal imperfect, third person masculine singular, agreeing with the collective singular subject זַרְעֲךָ.
analysis.sense: to be in a state or condition

analysis.evidence: Addressing Abram, God foretells that his descendants will live as foreigners in a land other than their own. The singular יִהְיֶה agrees with זַרְעֲךָ, while the plural לָהֶם and אֹתָם refer to the people collectively. In the covenant with Abram, these are his promised descendants.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular common noun in the construct state with a second-person masculine singular possessive suffix referring to Abram.
analysis.sense: the seed of the promise (to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob)

analysis.evidence: Abram’s descendants will live as strangers (גֵר) in a land described as לֹא לָהֶם, “not theirs.” אֶרֶץ denotes the territory where they will reside.
analysis.morphology: The locative preposition בְּ means “in.” אֶרֶץ is a common noun of both genders, singular and in the absolute state.
